title: Comparing and choosing
job: More, less, better — stating a preference
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: THE COMPARATIVE IS ONE ENDING plus a short list of irregulars, and the irregulars are the ones actually used: lúchshe, khúzhe, ból'she, mén'she, dorózhe, deshévle, výshe, molózhe. The ending is -yeye (interésneye), and the slogan it invites has to be killed: "add -yeye" produces khoroshéye, which is not a word. Learn the list as vocabulary and the ending as a rule.

"THAN" IS THE GENITIVE, and this is the level's fourth spend of M3's case: Moskvá ból'she Peterbúrga, On výshe menyá. It is what a Russian says, it is shorter, and it costs no new word at all. chem is the always-available alternative and becomes the required one when the two things compared are not both bare nouns — Segódnya teplée, chem vcherá.

The superlative is sámyy plus the adjective, and sámyy declines along with it: sámyy bol'shóy górod, sámaya interésnaya kníga. It is the easy half of the module and a rest point after the comparatives — two words, both agreeing, nothing irregular.

lúchshe serves BOTH khoroshó ("well") and khoróshiy ("good"), so On igráyet lúchshe and Éhtot chay lúchshe use one word for what English splits into "better" twice over. And the double comparative is the error even native speakers are teased for: bóleye lúchshe is wrong, because lúchshe is already the comparative.

éhtot is NOT L1-M1's éhto. éhto is "this is" and never changes; éhtot means "this" in front of a noun and declines with it — éhtot chay, éhta kníga, éhti knígi. Merging them would send every choice in the course to a note about identifying things. kakóy ("which, what kind of") declines like an adjective and is a sibling of L1-M9's chto, not a form of it.

words.note: A different word from L1-M1's éhto, which is "this is" and never changes. This one agrees with the noun it points at, exactly as an adjective does.
Irregular, and it does two jobs: better as a quality and better as a manner. English needs "better" for both too, which is the one place the two languages agree here.

sentences.trap: The neuter of éhtot is éhto, which is spelled exactly like L1-M1's pointing word. They are still two different words, and only the sentence around them says which is meant.
sentences.sound: EH-tat chay LUCH-she. The final o of éhtot reduces to a, which is why the two words sound less alike than they look.

variations.changed: feminine, so the pointing word moves
the opposite verdict
plural — one form for every gender

mistake.why: lúchshe is already comparative: Éhtot chay lúchshe.

sentences.usage: Choosing between two things in front of you.

words.note: The regular comparative: -yeye on the stem, and one form for every gender and number. Comparatives do not agree, which makes them the easiest thing in the module.
lúchshe's opposite, and irregular in the same way. It answers both plókho ("badly") and plokhóy ("bad").

sentences.trap: A comparative never agrees with anything. interésneye is the same word for a book, a film or two books — which is a genuine rest after M3's grid.
sentences.sound: EH-ta KNI-ga in-ti-RYES-ni-ye. The ending is two syllables and unstressed, so it trails off.

variations.changed: masculine — and the comparative does not move
an irregular comparative
plural — the comparative still does not move

mistake.why: A comparison needs the comparative: Éhta kníga interésneye.

words.note: M3's dorogóy with the g softened to zh. That consonant change is what makes so many comparatives look irregular when the ending is regular.
M3's deshyóvyy, and note the yó is GONE: the stress has moved, and a yó cannot be unstressed. The spelling records the sound.

sentences.trap: deshyóvyy becomes deshévle, losing its yó. That is not an exception to the yó rule — it is the rule: a yó is always stressed, so when the stress leaves, so does the yó.
sentences.sound: EH-tat bi-LYET da-RO-zhe. The zh is hard, which pulls the e after it back.

variations.changed: the opposite, and the yó disappears with the stress
feminine — the comparative is unchanged
M4's indeclinable noun, which changes nothing either

mistake.why: The one-word comparative is what is said: Éhtot bilét dorózhe.

sentences.usage: In a ticket office, comparing two options.
sentences.mnemonic: The stress leaves, the yó leaves with it.

sentences.cue: My brother is taller than me

words.note: M2's vysókiy, with the k softened to sh. It covers height of a person and of a building alike.
The word for "than", always available and required when the two things compared are not both bare nouns: Segódnya teplée, chem vcherá.

sentences.trap: There is no word for "than" here at all. The genitive menyá is the comparison — the fifth job M3's case does — and it is shorter and more idiomatic than the chem version beside it.
sentences.sound: moy brat VY-she mi-NYA. The y of výshe is the hard back vowel, and the sh in front of it keeps it there.

variations.cue: My brother is taller than I am
variations.changed: the chem version — correct, and a shade heavier

variations.cue: My sister is taller than me
variations.changed: a different subject; the comparative does not move

variations.cue: My brother is younger than me
variations.changed: a different comparison

mistake.why: Either the genitive or chem, not both: výshe menyá or výshe, chem ya.

sentences.usage: Comparing people, which in Russian is done with the genitive by default.

sentences.cue: My brother is younger than me

words.note: M2's molodóy with the d softened to zh and the stress pulled back onto the stem — two changes at once, which is why it is on the irregular list.
molózhe's opposite, and M2's stáryy behind it. Of people it is the ordinary word; stareye is used of things.

sentences.trap: molodóy is stressed on the ending and molózhe on the stem. The stress moves in most comparatives, and the mark is the only record of it.
sentences.sound: moy brat ma-LO-zhe mi-NYA. Only the first o of molózhe reduces; the stressed one is fully sounded.

variations.cue: My sister is younger than me
variations.changed: a different subject

variations.cue: He is younger than my brother
variations.changed: chem, because the second half is two words

variations.cue: My father is older than me
variations.changed: the opposite comparison

mistake.why: This one is irregular: Moy brat molózhe menyá.

sentences.usage: Placing family members by age, which is the first thing anyone asks.

sentences.cue: There is more water here than there

words.note: The comparative of both mnógo ("much") and bol'shóy ("big"), so it means "more" and "bigger" alike. Like mnógo, it takes the genitive.
ból'she's opposite, and doubled the same way: less and smaller. M3's málen'kiy has no separate comparative of its own.

sentences.trap: chem is required here because the second half is tam, not a noun. That is the line between the two "than" constructions, and it is the only rule about them worth carrying.
sentences.sound: zdyes' BOL'-she va-DY chem tam. The soft sign in ból'she is heard as a softening of the l.

variations.cue: There is less water here than there
variations.changed: the opposite quantity
no comparison stated, and still a genitive after it
ból'she meaning bigger rather than more

mistake.why: A word of amount takes the genitive: ból'she vodý.

sentences.usage: Comparing two places, two shops, two portions.
sentences.mnemonic: ból'she is more and bigger at once.

sentences.cue: This is the most interesting book

words.note: The superlative is two words and both agree with the noun. Nothing is irregular here — after the comparatives, this is the module's rest point.
The positive behind interésneye, with M3's four cells. The superlative needs the positive, not the comparative.

sentences.trap: sámyy takes the ordinary adjective after it, never the comparative. sámaya interésneye is wrong for the same reason bóleye lúchshe is — one comparison per phrase.
sentences.sound: EH-ta SA-ma-ya in-ti-RYES-na-ya KNI-ga. Four words, and the two long ones rhyme at the end.

variations.changed: masculine throughout

variations.cue: This is the most expensive book
variations.changed: a different quality
M3's adjective, with its yó back because the stress is back

mistake.why: The superlative takes the ordinary adjective: sámaya interésnaya kníga.

sentences.usage: Recommending the best of several — in a shop, a menu, a shelf.
sentences.mnemonic: Two words, both agreeing, nothing irregular.

words.note: It declines like an adjective and agrees with its noun. It is a sibling of L1-M9's chto, not a form of it — chto asks what a thing is, kakóy asks which one.
Takes an accusative noun or an infinitive. A long word, and the ordinary alternative is simply lúchshe — Chay lúchshe, tea is better.

sentences.trap: kakóy agrees, chto does not. Kakáya kníga? asks which book; Chto éhto? asks what a thing is, and they are never swapped.
sentences.sound: ka-KOY chay vy prit-pa-chi-TA-yi-tye. The verb is six syllables and only the fifth carries.

variations.changed: feminine, and L1-M9's frame
the answer, with an accusative noun
a comparative in the question

mistake.why: Choosing among things takes kakóy: Kakóy chay vy predpochitáyete?

sentences.usage: Offering a choice — in a shop, at a table, on a menu.
sentences.mnemonic: chto asks what. kakóy asks which.

sentences.display: Ya predpochitáyu chay, a ne kófe
sentences.script: Я предпочитаю чай, а не кофе
sentences.literal: I prefer tea, and not coffee

words.note: The vy cell. Its ty cell would be predpochitáyesh', with M6's -esh' ending — the pattern holds even on a word this long.

sentences.trap: a ne is the contrastive "not", not the plain one. L1-M10's a is "and" with a turn in it, and this is that same a doing the turning.
sentences.sound: ya prit-pa-chi-TA-yu chay a nye KO-fye. The a is unstressed and almost disappears into the pause.

variations.display: Ya predpochitáyu kófe, a ne chay
variations.script: Я предпочитаю кофе, а не чай

sentences.usage: Stating a preference clearly, which Russian does without hedging.

sentences.cue: This shop is better, but more expensive

words.note: Masculine, stem-stressed in the singular. Its plural moves the stress right off — gorodá — which is the same pattern as M4's poyezdá.

sentences.trap: Two comparatives on one subject and neither agrees with anything. After M3's grid this is genuinely easy, and saying so is part of the lesson.
sentences.sound: EH-tat ma-ga-ZIN LUCH-she no da-RO-zhe. The two comparatives both end in the same unstressed -e.
